overview: Western Australia developed from the Swan River settlement established in 1829. This map record covers its late colonial decades, including responsible government in 1890 and the gold rushes that drew many newcomers onto Aboriginal lands.

periods.title: Early settler colony
periods.summary: The Swan River colony struggled to attract and retain enough settlers for its ambitions.

periods.title: Convict labour and colonial expansion
periods.summary: Transported convicts built major public works; transportation ended in 1868, but its institutions remained.

periods.title: Self-government and gold rushes
periods.summary: A local ministry answered to parliament while gold discoveries accelerated settlement and investment.

items.text: Convicts built Fremantle’s prison from limestone quarried at the site during the 1850s. Other convict gangs worked on colonial infrastructure. More than 9,700 men were transported to Western Australia before transportation ended in 1868; their labour left highly visible buildings.

Convict James Roe described Fremantle in English: “Conspicuous above all rises the prison.” In plainer words, the prison stood out above everything else. Fremantle Prison reproduces his observation with his convict number, 6709, a view of the town from someone held there.

Pearlshell already had deep significance in Aboriginal exchange and ceremony. Carved riji shells circulated across northwestern and central Australia during the nineteenth century, valued for connections with water, rain and life. Colonial pearling entered an existing world of shell knowledge.

The pearling industry could be brutal: Aboriginal women were sometimes forced to dive. Later Asian workers also supplied skilled labour. The Western Australian Museum’s interpretation preserves this history alongside the attractive shells, so the industry’s beauty does not hide the people who suffered.

Discoveries at Coolgardie in 1892 and Kalgoorlie in 1893 brought a rush of migrants. Some found work rather than fortunes, and new businesses followed. Aboriginal communities experienced disease, dispossession and restricted access to precious water as the fields expanded.

Water was so scarce that prospectors used dryblowers to separate gold from soil rather than relying only on wet panning. The machine’s sifting action adapted prospecting to the dry environment. Gold hunting did not always involve the familiar image of a pan in a stream.

Many new arrivals lived in canvas shelters over wooden frames, with floors of sand or canvas. Packing cases and used kerosene tins became furniture. Wealthier mine managers could afford brick houses, giving the same goldfield very different levels of domestic comfort.

Heat, blowing dust, expensive fresh water and typhoid made family life difficult in the early goldfields towns. Tree cutting for mining, locomotives and water condensers worsened the dust. The practical challenge was getting through an ordinary day as well as finding gold.

The Coolgardie safe offered food cooling without electricity. Water soaked cloth around a cupboard; evaporation carried heat away. A breezy position helped it work. This technology appeared in the 1890s and remained useful in rural households well into the next century.

A food safe’s legs could stand in tins of water to discourage ants, while its covering kept flies and other animals away. Imagine a cupboard wearing wet clothes and standing in little moats: practical engineering for protecting dinner.

sections.title: Water, rights and a new federation

items.text: Goldfields residents pressed for reliable fresh water in the 1890s. The resulting pipeline eventually stretched more than 600 kilometres from the Perth region. It opened in 1903, after federation: an important colonial project whose benefits arrived in the state period.

Responsible government arrived in 1890, and legislation extended voting rights to women in 1899. Political equality remained incomplete: racial restrictions still excluded many Aboriginal people. The expanding settler electorate and the people displaced by settlement did not enjoy the same political power.

ending.text: Western Australia joined the Commonwealth on 1 January 1901 and became a state. Its 1900 referendum supported federation after prolonged debate. The imported 1900 endpoint belongs to this constitutional transition, not the disappearance of Western Australia or its peoples.
